title: Picking a layer leaves alone the settings that did not change
goal: Click something on the canvas and the settings panel on the right rebuilds every control in it, even when the thing you clicked has exactly the same settings as the thing you clicked before. That is the pause people feel when they click back and forth between two shapes: about two frames of work per click, all of it in the panel. The panel should leave a control alone when the number or the word it is showing has not changed, so picking feels instant.
notes:
SUCCESSOR to a-section-that-appears-in-the-right-hand-panel-a, which was dropped because its premise was wrong. The measurements are in the comment above `arrivals` in Sources/Photonz/InspectorPanel.swift and the walk that takes them is Scripts/playtest/perf/pick-cost-walk.json (kept out of Scripts/playtest so the sweep never runs a stopwatch). Measured 2026-09-17, probe build, longest single run loop pass per pick, median of 5, screen locked with PHOTONZ_ALLOW_LOCKED_WALK=1 so absolute numbers may be understated; every comparison is one variable at a time in the same session.

WHAT IS TRUE. Two identical arrows, picked back and forth: 33.4 / 35.1ms. A box and an arrow, which show the same SECTIONS but different rows: 25.9 / 39.0ms. So a pick that changes nothing about the panel's shape still costs two frames, and new rows arriving are only about 4ms of the 39.

WHERE IT IS. With PartsInspector's body replaced by a blank the arrow pick is 16.3ms and the box pick 18.5ms: the Appearance form is the whole difference. Inside it, taking out the three segmented picture pickers is worth 7ms, the five sliders 4ms, the number boxes beside them 3ms. No villain: roughly a millisecond per control that is handed a new value, and an arrow's Appearance hands out about twenty.

IT IS NOT THE NUMBER OF CONTROLS. Ten extra sliders added to Appearance, wrapped so their value never changes between picks, cost nothing at all (34.6 against 35.8). A control whose inputs are unchanged is free. That is the whole opening.

THE PRIZE AND THE HAZARD, both measured. Wrapping each part row in PartsInspector in an EquatableView keyed on what it draws took the arrow-to-arrow pick from 33.8 to 20.2ms. It ALSO put the other arrow's pick up to 51.6ms and left stale values on screen, because a skipped row keeps the closures it was built with and those name the layer that WAS picked. So the row cannot simply be wrapped: it has to stop carrying the selection in its closures first. A row should take the reading it shows (a value, already Equatable) plus enough to name WHAT it edits, and resolve which layers that reaches from EditorState at the moment the control is used. Then a stale-but-identical row is behaviourally identical, and the wrap is safe.

START AT PartsInspector.swift (the ForEach over layerPartRows), ShapePartSettings.swift and InspectorControls.swift (ShapeSlider, LayerStyleSlider, SliderReadout). LayerPartRow.id is already stable across selections, so the ForEach identity is not the problem.

TRIED AND WORTH NOTHING, do not repeat: caching the segmented pickers' pictures (PathLineStyleGlyph, ArrowheadStyle.glyph) so they are drawn once instead of per pick. Changed nothing measurable (35.6 against 35.8), because NSImage(size:flipped:) defers its drawing block anyway. The 7ms those rows cost is the NSSegmentedControl being updated, not the pictures being made.
acceptance: Picking between two identical arrows costs no more than 22ms of main thread work in its longest single pass, down from 33 to 35ms today, measured with Scripts/playtest/perf/pick-cost-walk.json

A control the pick left alone still edits the layer that is NOW picked: straight after clicking from one arrow to another, changing Ending, Thickness and Opacity each changes the arrow that was clicked last, and nothing happens to the other one
Nothing shows a stale reading: after picking a thin arrow and then a thick one, Thickness reads the thick one's number
arrow-parts-walk, parts-settings-inline-walk and picker-controls-walk behave exactly as they do on main before the change, run before and after
